newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Police can safely control HK without PLA - general.
newsitem.headline: Police can safely control HK without PLA - general.

text.p: Chinese troops garrisoned here after Hong Kong reverts to China will face no military challenge because local police can adequately maintain security, the commander of outgoing British forces said on Thursday.

"I genuinely believe that there is nothing likely to occur in Hong Kong in the forthcoming years that isn't well within the capability of the Hong Kong police," Major-General Bryan Dutton told reporters at Hong Kong's Foreign Correspondents' Club.
Hong Kong, a territory of 6.4 million people coming under Beijing's rule from July 1, is one of the world's safest cities, with a modern, 27,000-strong paramilitary police.

"They've a very large force, " said Dutton. "They've been quite deliberately developed over the last decade to make them quite self- sufficient. They handle internal security problems, law and order and the patrolling of the borders of Hong Kong in a very satisfactory and professional way."
As for the People's Liberation Army (PLA) role, Dutton said: "Their military task is a limited one. There is no external threat to Hong Kong."
Dutton is the 61st commander of British forces in Hong Kong since the territory was first garrisoned 156 years ago.

His troops have dwindled to about 1,200 in preparation for the handover to China at midnight on June 30. An advance party of about 200 soldiers from the PLA has already taken up residence in Hong Kong and will be substantially reinforced on July 1.
Dutton said the main rationale for China sending PLA troops into Hong Kong was to demonstrate sovereignty over the territory after what some in Beijing view as a humiliating colonial interlude.

He said the PLA is sending to Hong Kong its best troops, kitted out with the finest uniforms and equipment, in hopes of rehabilitating a reputation tarnished by the army's June 4, 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
At full strength Britain kept 10,000 troops in Hong Kong and China is expected to allot roughly the same number.

Speaking of the post-handover period in Hong Kong, which some fear might lead to a significant curtailment of civil and economic liberties, Dutton sounded an optimistic note while acknowledging "there is plenty of potential for misunderstanding."
"I hope it will work and I hope there won't be problems. There is practical evidence of their (the PLA) sincere intent," the general said.

"The PLA must be given credit for this but only in the way in which you give a man credit for having the underlying desire to make a New Year's resolution. Belief and respect comes when in the following months and years we find he has held true to his intentions."
Dutton insisted that Britain's strategic interest in Asia would not be diminished by the handover of Hong Kong.
"Britain remains the single largest European investor in China with major investments throughout the region quite apart from its interests in Hong Kong," the British general told reporters.

"Our interests are continuing and expanding. These economic facts mean that Britain must engage in Asia and must remain engaged in Asia. There will be concern in the future to ensure that it remains a stable region to do business and that our interests are safeguarded.
Dutton said the main means of ensuring Britain's interests in Asia in the future would be political rather than military.
